intro: On the night of 29 December 1940, German bombs burned out Cripplegate. Thirty years later a new town stood on the ruins: 2,014 flats on a raised deck, terraces round a lake, and three towers that stayed London's tallest homes for 30 years. The City of London paid for it, built it and still runs it.
story: AD 90
The Romans build a fort here. A barbican is a watchtower on a city wall, and the name stuck.
A single night of bombing on 29 December burns out most of the district.
Only 48 people still live in Cripplegate.
Three young architects enter a competition for the Golden Lane estate next door. They agree that whoever wins will bring in the other two. Geoffry Powell wins.
The City asks Chamberlin, Powell and Bon to plan the bombed land to the south.
The City decides the site will be homes for people who work in the City, not offices.
The architects' report sets out the scheme that gets built: a raised deck, terraces, a lake and towers.
The Underground moves into a new tunnel that sits on rubber pads, so trains don't shake the flats.
The first tenants move into Speed House.
Cromwell Tower is finished.
Lauderdale Tower is finished.
Shakespeare Tower, the last block, is finished. The estate took seven years to build.
Right to Buy reaches the estate. Tenants can buy 125-year leases, most starting in 1981.
The Queen opens the Barbican Centre on 3 March. There are fireworks over the lake.
All but about 300 flats now belong to the people who live in them.
The whole estate is listed Grade II. Two years later its gardens are listed Grade II*.
The top floors of Frobisher Crescent, offices for decades, become 69 flats.
The YMCA on Fann Street becomes Blake Tower, 74 flats.
Plans to renew the Barbican Centre are approved. Work starts in 2027.
built: People walk on a raised deck one to three floors up. Cars, deliveries and parking stay underneath, out of sight.
Builders poured the concrete, let it cure for four weeks, then attacked it by hand with picks and hammers. That exposes the granite chips inside and gives the walls their rough grey grain.
Each tower is a triangle with three flats a floor and a lift in the middle. The plans grew from 30 floors in 1956 to more than 40 by 1961.

Most kitchens had a Garchey sink. You put wet rubbish, tins and bottles down the plughole. It travelled through two miles of tunnels to 150 pits, and a tanker sucked it out. More than 1,400 still worked in 2004.
Electric cables run through the floors and warm every flat from October to April. Residents can't turn it off.
Four tracks once ran through the site in an open cutting. The engineers boxed them into a 305 m tunnel on rubber bearings.
The Conservatory sits on top of the theatre, partly to hide the theatre's tall fly tower. It now holds about 1,500 kinds of plant, plus fish and terrapins.
Pieces of the Roman and medieval city wall still stand in the gardens, next to the church of St Giles Cripplegate, which survived the bombing.
people: The driving force of the three. He ran the theatre design and died two years after the last tower opened, before the arts centre was finished.
Won the Golden Lane competition that started the firm. He later said of the Barbican, "in the end it killed our practice".
Swiss, trained in Zurich and Milan. He led the arts centre with Chamberlin and took over the theatre after he died.
Worked out how to build on London clay and how to stop the trains shaking the flats.
Designed the lettering and signs around the estate, including the small castle mark for the Roman watchtower.
Paid for the estate, built it and still runs it. It called the arts centre the City's gift to the nation.
facts: Every tower lift has a small hatch into each flat's service cupboard, so the milk and post could be left without anyone knocking.
The Queen Mother planted a mulberry tree in Thomas More Garden in 1984.
The old stump on the highwalk came from a 500-year-old beech in Burnham Beeches that fell in 1990. The City owns that forest too.
The arts centre was meant to cost about £14 million. By 1982 it had cost about £159 million.
On opening night 3,500 guests watched fireworks over the lake, and BBC2 showed the whole evening live.
A gold refiner's frieze from a bombed shop at 53 Barbican was saved in 1962. It now stands at a west entrance to the estate.
The towers turn up in One of Our Dinosaurs Is Missing, a 1975 Disney film set in the 1920s.
The estate has played MI6 in Quantum of Solace and the planet Coruscant in Andor.
Unit 4 + 2 shot a film for their song Concrete and Clay on the building site in 1965.
In 2003 residents were offered the chance to run the estate themselves. They voted no, by a wide margin.
